title: Restoring Microcirculation Through Integrative Orthomolecular Systems Medicine—A Root Cause Framework Integrating Metabolic Nutrition Orthomolecular Support and Neuroendocrine Regulation
content: Microcirculatory dysfunction can limit tissue delivery of oxygen and nutrients even when large arteries remain patent. A treatment strategy directed only at vasodilation may leave the metabolic, nutritional, inflammatory, structural, and neuroendocrine causes of impaired perfusion unresolved. This perspective proposes an Integrative Orthomolecular Systems Medicine (I-OM) framework for restoring microvascular function. A focused narrative review of human physiological studies and intervention trials informs the framework; it is not a systematic review. The approach combines individualized metabolic nutrition, orthomolecular support, physical activity, sleep and stress regulation, and treatment of identifiable disease and exposure-related drivers. Nicotinic acid is a central example of a nutrient with therapeutic actions beyond deficiency correction: small human studies demonstrate improvements in resistance-vessel responsiveness, while vitamin C studies support reversible oxidative impairment of endothelial function. Magnesium and exercise provide additional evidence of functional or structural vascular effects. Evidence varies substantially across tissues, formulations, populations, and endpoints. The insulin–cortisol–vitamin C framework is used as an organizing hypothesis rather than an established unified mechanism. The proposed clinical sequence is to identify the affected vascular phenotype, examine limiting factors, reconnect interacting systems, and intervene with measurable goals. The complete I-OM package has not been tested in a controlled trial, and synergy cannot be assumed from separate component studies. Prospective studies should combine direct microvascular measurements with symptoms, function, safety, and organ-specific outcomes.
